issues.legal_issue: A lifetime wakf of property governed by a special estate statute is a transfer subject to that statute’s limits.
material_facts: The disputed property included a talukdari estate governed by a special statutory scheme.
The estate holder executed a wakf during his lifetime, dedicating the property for himself and his family and descendants.
issues.conclusion: The wakf was a transfer of the estate property and its validity had to be determined under the statutory powers and restrictions governing that property.
issues.legal_principle: The Oudh Estates Act was a self-contained code governing the rights of talukdars in the estates it covered. Under sections 2 and 11, a wakf is a lifetime transfer in the nature of a gift and is valid only within the powers conferred by the Act. The Court relied on Chandra Kishore Pewari v. Sissendi Estate for the character of the Act as a complete code, and explained that sections 3 and 4 of the Mussalman Wakf Validating Act, 1913, did not displace the limits imposed by the Oudh Estates Act.

predicates.estate_rights_dispute: The case concerned competing claims to property governed by special rules for estate rights and succession.
predicates.estate_property_governed_by_special_tran: The property at issue was an estate subject to a statutory scheme regulating its transfer.
predicates.lifetime_wakf_created: The estate holder dedicated the property by wakf during his lifetime.

issues.definition: When an estate-rights dispute concerns property governed by special transfer rules and a wakf created during the holder’s lifetime, the wakf is subject to those rules.

issues.legal_issue: A wakf chiefly benefiting the settlor’s descendants does not qualify as a gift to religious or charitable uses merely because it provides for limited charity or ultimately directs property to charity.
material_facts: The wakf devoted only an insignificant part of the income to religious or charitable purposes during the family’s existence.
Most of the income was directed to the settlor and his descendants from generation to generation.
The broader charitable or religious application of the income was postponed until the family line became extinct.
issues.conclusion: The wakf was not a gift to religious or charitable uses within section 18 of the Oudh Estates Act; section 18 prescribed the procedure for such gifts and did not exempt them from section 12.
issues.legal_principle: The Court construed “religious or charitable uses” in section 18 in the context of an Act applying to talukdars of all religions; provision for one’s descendants was not such a use. Section 18 dealt with the procedure for gifts of that kind, while the power to make gifts arose under section 11, and section 12 applied to transfers under the Act. Sections 3 and 4 of the Mussalman Wakf Validating Act, 1913, validated wakfs-alal-aulad in specified circumstances but did not make family support itself a religious or charitable purpose under section 18. The Court considered Bikani Mia v. Shuklal Poddar and relied on the Privy Council’s decision in Abul Fata Mahomed Ishak v. Russomoy Dhur Chowdry.

predicates.estate_transfer_validity_dispute: The case concerned whether a transfer of regulated estate property was valid.
predicates.family_descendants_are_primary_beneficia: The deed directed the main benefit of the property’s income to the settlor and descendants over generations.
predicates.charitable_use_is_insignificant_or_postp: The deed provided only limited charitable or religious use while the family survived and reserved broader such use until the family line ended.

issues.definition: In a dispute over a regulated estate transfer, a wakf chiefly benefiting descendants and providing only insignificant or postponed charity is not a family-benefit wakf for religious or charitable use.

issues.legal_issue: A wakf violates the statutory rule against perpetuity when absolute vesting, including beneficial enjoyment of the property and its usufruct, is postponed beyond the permitted period.
material_facts: The deed directed the property’s income principally to family members over successive generations.

Although the property was said to vest immediately in God, God had no beneficial ownership for generations, and the family’s enjoyment of the income continued without a limit tied to the statutory vesting period.
The property was governed by the Oudh Estates Act, and the validity of the wakf was challenged in a dispute over succession and possession.
issues.conclusion: The wakf was invalid under section 12 of the Oudh Estates Act because the absolute vesting contemplated by that section was postponed beyond the permitted period.
issues.legal_principle: Section 12 of the Oudh Estates Act barred a transfer or bequest that delayed vesting beyond the period specified in that section. The majority held that “vesting” meant absolute vesting, comprising both legal and beneficial ownership, including the ability to deal with the property and its usufruct. Immediate legal dedication did not suffice where beneficial enjoyment remained tied up for generations. The Court also referred to Underhill’s Law of Trusts and Trustees on the rule against perpetuities. Sections 3 and 4 of the Mussalman Wakf Validating Act, 1913, did not alter this result.

predicates.challenge_to_validity_of_estate_wakf: The case was a challenge to the validity of a wakf affecting property governed by special estate rules.
predicates.estate_property_governed_by_special_tran: The property subject to the wakf was regulated by statutory rules governing its transfer.
predicates.family_enjoyment_continues_over_generati: The deed provides for family members to enjoy the property’s income over successive generations.
predicates.absolute_beneficial_vesting_is_delayed: The person in whom legal title is said to vest cannot freely deal with the property and its income because beneficial enjoyment remains reserved for others beyond the permitted period.

issues.definition: If a challenged wakf of specially regulated estate property reserves enjoyment to a family over generations and thereby delays absolute beneficial vesting, the wakf is invalid for that delay.

issues.legal_issue: A person claiming possession solely as mutawalli cannot retain possession when the wakf on which that office depends is invalid.
material_facts: The person in possession claimed a right to remain there as mutawalli under the wakf deed.
The wakf was held invalid, and the claimant’s right to possession depended on his office under that wakf.
issues.conclusion: The claimant could not remain in possession as mutawalli once the wakf failed, and the decree granting possession to the person entitled under the applicable succession rule was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: The right to possession asserted as mutawalli depended on the validity of the wakf creating that office. Once the wakf failed, that basis for possession failed with it.

predicates.possession_claimed_only_as_mutawalli: The person in possession relied on appointment as mutawalli as the basis for remaining in possession.
predicates.underlying_wakf_is_invalid: The wakf deed on which the claimed office depends has been held invalid.
predicates.dispute_concerns_entitlement_to_possessi: The case requires a court to determine who is entitled to possess the property.

issues.definition: When possession is claimed only as mutawalli, the wakf is invalid, and entitlement to possession is disputed, the claimant cannot retain possession under that wakf.
